passages.happening:
Hannah has given her son to the LORD, and now she sings. “My heart rejoices in the LORD in whom my horn is exalted. My mouth speaks boldly against my enemies, for I rejoice in Your salvation” (verse 1).

“There is no one holy like the LORD. Indeed, there is no one besides You! And there is no Rock like our God” (verse 2). The proud are told to stop boasting, for the LORD knows, and he weighs what people do (verse 3).

Then the song turns the world over. The bows of the mighty are broken and the feeble are given strength. The well-fed work for bread and the hungry are filled. ‘The barren woman gives birth to seven, but she who has many sons pines away’ (verse 5). “The LORD brings death and gives life; He brings down to Sheol and raises up. The LORD sends poverty and wealth; He humbles and He exalts” (verses 6-7). He lifts the poor from the dust and seats them among princes (verse 8).

The song ends far beyond Hannah's own life: “The LORD will judge the ends of the earth and will give power to His king. He will exalt the horn of His anointed” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
This is Hebrew poetry, built on pairs of lines and sharp contrasts: the mighty and the feeble, the full and the hungry, the barren woman and the mother of many, death and life. It moves from Hannah's own praise to a picture of who God is, and ends with his judgment of the earth and his king.

The horn was the horn of a wild ox, held high. To have your horn exalted meant strength, honor and victory. The song opens with Hannah's horn lifted and closes with the horn of the LORD's anointed, so one woman's vindication frames the future strength of Israel's king.

Rock is an old name for God in Hebrew poetry. It pictures a place of refuge and stability. Sheol is the grave, the place of the dead. Even there God's rule reaches.

The song raises a question. It speaks of a king and his anointed, but Israel had no king in Hannah's day. Some scholars think an existing royal psalm was placed in her mouth by the book's author because it suited the moment. Others hold that Hannah spoke as a prophet. Either way, in its place the song works as an overture to the whole book. Every rise and fall that follows, Eli's and Samuel's, Saul's and David's, is sung here first.

The last word of the song, anointed, is mashiach in Hebrew. This is the first time in the Bible that it is used of a king. It gives English the word messiah.
passages.later:
Near the end of 2 Samuel stands David's song, which shares many of the same pictures: “My God is my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield, and the horn of my salvation” (2 Samuel 22:3), and ‘The LORD thundered from heaven’ (2 Samuel 22:14). Many scholars see the two songs as deliberate bookends.

A psalm repeats Hannah's words almost exactly: “He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the dump” (Psalm 113:7).

And Mary's song in Luke is woven from Hannah's. Hannah sang that the LORD ‘humbles and He exalts’. Mary sings, “He has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble” (Luke 1:52).
passages.asks: Hannah's song says that God raises the poor and humbles the proud. Ask where you have seen that pattern, in Scripture, in history or in a life you know. And ask which side of the song you are tempted to stand on: the side that boasts, or the side that waits to be lifted.

passages.t: The priests who took, and the boy who served
passages.happening:
Elkanah goes home to Ramah, ‘but the boy began ministering to the LORD before Eli the priest’ (verse 11).

The priests are another matter. ‘Now the sons of Eli were wicked men; they had no regard for the LORD’ (verse 12). When anyone offers a sacrifice, their servant comes with a three-pronged fork while the meat is boiling, plunges it into the pot, and the priest takes whatever it brings up (verses 13-14). Worse, before the fat is burned on the altar, the servant demands raw meat. If a worshiper objects that the fat must be burned first, the servant answers, “No, you must give it to me right now. If you refuse, I will take it by force!” (verse 16).

“Thus the sin of these young men was severe in the sight of the LORD, for they were treating the LORD’s offering with contempt” (verse 17).

Meanwhile Samuel serves before the LORD, a small boy in a linen ephod (verse 18). Each year his mother makes him a little robe and brings it when she comes for the sacrifice (verse 19). Eli prays for Elkanah and his wife: “May the LORD give you children by this woman in place of the one she dedicated to the LORD” (verse 20). The LORD attends to Hannah, and she has three more sons and two daughters. ‘Meanwhile, the boy Samuel grew up in the presence of the LORD’ (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Israel's law set out what belonged to whom. The fat of a peace offering belonged to the LORD and had to be burned on the altar first, and the priest received set portions, the breast and the right thigh. Eli's sons break both rules. They take whatever the fork brings up, they demand meat before God has received his share, and they threaten force.

Most people rarely ate meat except at a sacrifice. So this was theft from worshipers as well as contempt for God. The people who came to Shiloh to give thanks went home robbed by the men who served the altar.

The narrator tells this part of the chapter by turns: the sons' sin, then Samuel serving; the sons' sin again, then Samuel growing. The contrast does the teaching. Hannah's family gives to God, and the priestly family takes from him.

The linen ephod was a simple priestly garment, not the high priest's ornate one. The little robe each year is a mother's love that kept going after the parting.
passages.later:
The prophets spoke against leaders who served themselves instead of the people. Ezekiel was told to say, “Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves! Should not the shepherds feed their flock?” (Ezekiel 34:2).

And the law the sons ignored was plain: ‘All the fat is the LORD’s’ (Leviticus 3:16).
passages.asks: Eli's sons used God's house to feed themselves. Ask where religion can become a way to take instead of to serve, in a church or in your own heart. And ask who has served you faithfully in small ways, as Hannah did with her yearly robe, and whether you have thanked them.

passages.t: Eli's rebuke, and a boy who grew
passages.happening:
Eli is very old. He hears everything his sons are doing to all Israel, and that they are sleeping with the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting (verse 22).

He speaks to them. “Why are you doing these things?” Eli said to his sons. “I hear about your wicked deeds from all these people” (verse 23). “If a man sins against another man, God can intercede for him; but if a man sins against the LORD, who can intercede for him?” (verse 25).

‘But they would not listen to their father, since the LORD intended to put them to death’ (verse 25).

“And the boy Samuel continued to grow in stature and in favor with the LORD and with man” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
The women who served at the entrance to the tent are mentioned once before, in Exodus. What their work was is not known. What Eli's sons did to them is clear enough. The priests charged with guarding the holiness of God's house used their place to exploit the women who served there.

Eli's rebuke is real, and it is weak. He hears about it from others, he asks why, and he warns them. But he does not stop them. The next chapter gives God's verdict on that: ‘his sons blasphemed God and he did not restrain them’ (3:13).

His own words are true. A wrong done to another person can be brought to God, but who will plead for someone who sins against God himself? His sons do not listen.

Then the chapter turns back to the boy. Samuel grows in the same house, at the same altar, and grows in favor with God and with people.
passages.later:
The women ‘who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting’ appear in Exodus, where their bronze mirrors were made into the basin for the tabernacle (Exodus 38:8).

Luke closes his account of Jesus' boyhood with words that echo verse 26: “And Jesus grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man” (Luke 2:52). Samuel too grew up in God's house, and Luke's readers would see the line running from Hannah's son to Mary's.
passages.hard:
What does it mean that Eli's sons would not listen ‘since the LORD intended to put them to death’?

The verse seems to say that God's purpose to judge the sons was the reason they ignored their father. Were they then responsible? Readers have answered in several ways. Many see the same pattern as the hardening of Pharaoh in Exodus: after long and deliberate sin, God confirms people in the way they have chosen, so their refusal is both their own act and part of his judgment. Others note that the Hebrew can be read more loosely, as describing the outcome rather than the cause. Others read it as the narrator's way of saying that the time to turn back had passed.

On every reading the text holds the sons fully to account. Their sin is described in detail, called very great, and treated as contempt for the LORD. The Bible often holds together God's rule over judgment and people's responsibility for their sin without explaining how they fit, and this verse is one place it does.

The chapter also says something plain about what the sons did. Men with religious power used it to take from the people they served and to exploit the women who served beside them, and God called it sin. The site's page on abuse and its cover-up draws on these chapters: the faith demands the truth told, the abuser handed to the authorities, and the harmed believed and protected.

If you have been harmed by a controlling leader or church, what was done was wrong, and it was not your fault. Being taken in by someone who seemed godly is not a sign of weak faith. You are free to step away and to tell someone you trust. If you were abused in other ways, or a crime was done, it should be reported to the authorities. A pastor or counsellor outside that church may help you sort out what happened. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Eli disapproved of what his sons did, but he did not stop them. Ask where you have spoken against a wrong and then let it go on, at home, at work or in a church. And ask what it would take to act, and whom you would need to tell.

passages.t: A man of God, and the end of Eli's house
passages.happening:
A man of God comes to Eli with a word from the LORD. God had chosen Eli's ancestors in Egypt to be his priests, to offer sacrifices, burn incense and wear the ephod, and he had given them a share of the offerings (verses 27-28).

“Why then do you kick at My sacrifice and offering that I have prescribed for My dwelling place? You have honored your sons more than Me by fattening yourselves with the best of all the offerings of My people Israel” (verse 29).

God had said that Eli's house would serve him forever. “But now the LORD declares: Far be it from Me! For I will honor those who honor Me, but those who despise Me will be disdained” (verse 30).

The days are coming when no one in Eli's house will reach old age (verses 31-33). The sign will be this: his two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, will both die on the same day (verse 34). “Then I will raise up for Myself a faithful priest. He will do whatever is in My heart and mind” (verse 35). And those left in Eli's house will come begging for a priestly job and a piece of bread (verse 36).
passages.hearers:
Israel's priests were descended from Aaron, and Eli's family held the priesthood at Shiloh. The man of God reaches back to their calling in Egypt. Their privilege was a gift, and it came with a charge.

The word honor runs through the chapter. In Hebrew its root means heavy or weighty. God lifts the poor to a throne of honor (verse 8). Eli honors his sons more than God, and the family fattens itself on the offerings. Now God says he will honor those who honor him. In chapter 4 the same root returns, when the glory departs from Israel and Eli, who was heavy, falls to his death.

The promise to Eli's house had not been a blank check. God's ‘Far be it from Me’ shows that the priests could not hold God to his word while they held his worship in contempt.

The judgment unfolds in stages across Israel's history. Hophni and Phinehas die on one day in chapter 4. Later Saul has the priests of Nob, Eli's descendants, killed (chapter 22), and only Abiathar escapes. When Solomon becomes king, he removes Abiathar from the priesthood. Zadok, who had served beside Abiathar under David, became the leading priest of Solomon's temple, and his line held that office for centuries. Many readers identify Zadok and his line as the faithful priest of verse 35, and some see Samuel as a first fulfillment.

The faithful priest will walk before ‘My anointed one’ (verse 35). The king of Hannah's song appears again, though there is still no king in Israel.
passages.later: The word against Eli's house came true in Solomon's day: “So Solomon banished Abiathar from the priesthood of the LORD and thus fulfilled the word that the LORD had spoken at Shiloh against the house of Eli” (1 Kings 2:27).
passages.asks: ‘I will honor those who honor Me.’ Ask what it looks like to honor God in ordinary work and worship, and not to use religion for your own gain. And ask where a privilege you were given has begun to feel like something you are owed.
